claim: The primate retina contains on the order of 20 morphologically and physiologically distinct classes of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: Though only a few classes of light-sensitive cells capture the retinal image in the primate eye, evolution has produced many more classes of retinal ganglion cell (RGC), on the order of 20, each morphologically and physiologically distinct and independently tiling the retina, to convey visual information to the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about primate retinal anatomy and physiology.

claim: Each class of RGC independently tiles the retina.
source: Though only a few classes of light-sensitive cells capture the retinal image in the primate eye, evolution has produced many more classes of retinal ganglion cell (RGC), on the order of 20, each morphologically and physiologically distinct and independently tiling the retina, to convey visual information to the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RGC organization.

claim: The diversity of RGCs reflects complex early processing in the mammalian retina that was previously thought to reside deeper in the brain.
source: This dramatic expansion of cell classes in the retinal output, combined with microelectrode recordings in excised tissue, has made it increasingly clear that the diversity of RGCs reflects instead a surprising amount of complex early processing in the mammalian retina, processing that had previously been thought to reside deeper in the brain (Gollisch and Meister, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gollisch and Meister, 2010.

claim: There are specialized retinal circuits that convey directional selectivity (DS).
source: There is evidence, for example, for specialized circuits that convey directional selectivity (DS) (Barlow et al., 1964), segregate object from background motion (Lettvin et al., 1959), and anticipate moving stimuli (Berry et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barlow et al., 1964.

claim: There are specialized retinal circuits that segregate object from background motion.
source: There is evidence, for example, for specialized circuits that convey directional selectivity (DS) (Barlow et al., 1964), segregate object from background motion (Lettvin et al., 1959), and anticipate moving stimuli (Berry et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lettvin et al., 1959.

claim: There are specialized retinal circuits that anticipate moving stimuli.
source: There is evidence, for example, for specialized circuits that convey directional selectivity (DS) (Barlow et al., 1964), segregate object from background motion (Lettvin et al., 1959), and anticipate moving stimuli (Berry et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berry et al., 1999.

claim: Ex vivo recordings of RGCs are often made in excised retina detached from downstream visual pathways.
source: However, we remain uncertain about the direct functional role of these RGC classes because, while ex vivo recordings can characterize the specific stimulus requirements of RGC classes, they are often made in the excised retina that is detached from the downstream visual pathways they serve.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of ex vivo recording methods.

claim: Ex vivo recordings preclude direct manipulations of RGC activity to observe the impact on visual experience or behavior in the awake primate.
source: Such studies preclude direct manipulations of RGC activity to observe the impact on visual experience or behavior in the awake primate.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the ex vivo recording approach.

claim: Direction-selective (DS) cells have been recently observed in the non-human primate.
source: For example, we cannot say with certainty whether the DS cells recently observed in the non-human primate (NHP) are involved in eye movements, the perceptual experience of motion, or both.
evidence: This is stated as a recent observation in NHP research.

claim: There is lingering controversy about the perceptual roles of midget and parasol ganglion cells.
source: Indeed, there is even lingering controversy about the perceptual roles of the most common primate RGCs, the midget and parasol ganglion cells (Freedland and Rieke, 2022; Patterson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Freedland and Rieke, 2022 and Patterson et al., 2019.

claim: Midget and parasol ganglion cells are the most common primate RGCs.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about primate RGC populations.
